cards.text: Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles in the land of the Chaldeans (Ezekiel 1:1-3), gets another word from the LORD. God tells him, 'Son of man, confront Jerusalem with her abominations.' Buckle up, friend. This one's heavy, and God starts it at the very beginning.

cards.question: God goes all the way back to Jerusalem's beginning, before she was a city of His people. Where does He say her origin and birth were?

answers.text: In the land of the Canaanites

cards.text: God says her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite. Not exactly the family tree you frame and hang over the fireplace.
Then God describes the day she was born. And friend, it does NOT go the way a birth is supposed to go.

cards.question: On the day Jerusalem was born, someone at least washed her and wrapped her in cloths.

cards.text: Her cord wasn't cut. No washing, no salt, no cloths, and not one person cared enough to do even one of those things for her.

cards.question: Nobody cares for newborn Jerusalem. So what happens to her instead?

answers.text: She is thrown out into the open field
She is left at the city gate
She is set adrift on the river

cards.text: She was despised on the day she was born. Then God passes by and sees her lying there in her blood.

cards.question: God sees baby Jerusalem lying in her blood in the open field. What does He do?

answers.text: He sends her back to her parents

cards.text: 'Live!' God says it twice. Then He makes her thrive like a plant of the field.

cards.question: The baby God rescued grows up and becomes very ___, but she is still naked and bare.

cards.text: Then God passes by again, and she's old enough for love. He spreads His cloak over her and covers her.

cards.question: God has covered Jerusalem with His cloak. How does He make her His own?

answers.text: He enters into a covenant with her
He buys her from her parents
He wins her in a contest

cards.text: He bathes her, rinses off her blood, and dresses her in embroidered cloth, fine linen and silk. Friend, the fanciest thing I own is this apron, and it came with FLOUR on it.

cards.question: After the bracelets, the chain, the nose ring and the earrings, what does God put on Jerusalem's head?

cards.text: With gold and silver, and fine flour, honey and oil to eat, the baby from the open field rises to be queen. Me? I went from a bakery's clearance bin to a junk drawer, so I was headed the WRONG way.

cards.question: Queen Jerusalem's beauty stays a secret that only God knows about.
Jerusalem's fame spreads among the nations because her beauty is perfect. Where does that perfect beauty come from?

cards.text: Jerusalem is a famous queen now. But friend, this is where the story turns.

cards.question: Because of her fame, what does Queen Jerusalem start trusting in?

cards.text: She plays the harlot, and her beauty is there for anyone who passes by. She even takes some of the clothes God gave her and makes colorful high places for herself.

cards.question: Jerusalem keeps turning God's gifts into something else. What does she make out of the gold and silver jewelry He gave her?

cards.text: She drapes her embroidered garments over those idols. Then she sets God's oil and incense in front of them.

cards.question: Even the fine flour, oil and honey God fed Jerusalem ends up set before her idols.

cards.text: Then God asks her, 'Was your prostitution not enough?' Because she goes even further, with the sons and daughters she bore to Him.

cards.question: What does Jerusalem do with the sons and daughters she bore to God?

answers.text: She sends them off to Egypt
She hides them in the field

cards.text: God calls them 'My children.' And through all of it, Jerusalem doesn't remember something.

cards.question: Through all her unfaithfulness, what does God say Jerusalem never remembered?

answers.text: The days when she lay in her blood
The songs she sang as a queen
The names of all her neighbors

cards.text: Then God cries out, 'Woe! Woe to you,' and her shrines start going up.

cards.question: Jerusalem keeps her mounds and lofty shrines tucked away where nobody can see them.

cards.text: There's a lofty shrine in every public square and at the head of every street. Then she turns to the nations around her.

cards.question: Which of Jerusalem's neighbors does God name first as her lovers?

cards.text: God says she did it to provoke Him to anger. So He stretches out His hand against her and reduces her portion.

cards.question: God gives Jerusalem over to the daughters of the Philistines, who hate her. How do they feel about the way she's acting?

cards.text: Egypt? Not enough. So she turns to the Assyrians. And the Assyrians? STILL not enough.

cards.question: When she reaches out to Chaldea, the land of merchants, Jerusalem is finally satisfied.

cards.text: 'How weak-willed is your heart,' God says. He calls her an adulterous wife who takes in strangers instead of her own husband.

cards.question: In God's picture, prostitutes get paid. What does He say Jerusalem does instead?

answers.text: She pays her lovers to come to her
She demands gold and silver from them
She sends every one of them away

cards.text: Now comes the 'therefore.' God says she poured out her wealth and exposed herself to her lovers and her detestable idols.

cards.question: God names one more reason judgment is coming on Jerusalem. What is it?

cards.text: So God says He'll gather a crowd against her from all around.

cards.question: Who does God say He'll gather against Jerusalem?

cards.text: Those she loved and those she hated, all of them, and He'll expose her before them. Then God names her sentence.

cards.question: God sentences Jerusalem to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood.

cards.text: Then God hands her over to those very same lovers.

cards.question: What do Jerusalem's lovers do to the mounds and lofty shrines she built?

cards.text: They strip off her clothes, take her fine jewelry and leave her naked and bare. That's the same 'naked and bare' she was before God ever clothed her.

cards.question: Once they've taken everything, Jerusalem's lovers leave her alone.

cards.text: A mob comes with stones and swords. They burn down her houses in the sight of many women.

cards.question: God says He'll put an end to Jerusalem's prostitution, and she will never again ___ her lovers.
After all this judgment, God says He'll stay angry with Jerusalem forever.

cards.text: That line again: she did not remember the days of her youth, so God will bring her deeds down upon her own head. And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend, because God isn't done talking to Jerusalem.

findings.problem: The opening card has 4 sentences: 'Ezekiel... gets another word from the LORD.' / 'God tells him, ...' / 'Buckle up, friend.' / 'This one's heavy, and God starts it at the very beginning.'

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke 'Not exactly the family tree you frame and hang over the fireplace' gets its laugh from Amorite and Hittite ancestry being something to be embarrassed about. That makes the punchline a put-down of a people group.

rule.text: Never puts down any person or group: no jokes about age, gender, race, nationality, accents, appearance, intelligence or church denomination.

findings.problem: The setup line 'it does NOT go the way a birth is supposed to go' rules out 'True' on the next card, which asks whether someone washed her and wrapped her in cloths. The setup gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Card 10 says God makes her 'thrive like a plant of the field.' That rules out the wrong answer 'sickly' before the baker reaches the blank.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The joke says his apron 'came with FLOUR on it.' The backstory says that when he was renewed, his apron was clean. The joke contradicts the established Dorinverse story.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The joke 'I went from a bakery's clearance bin to a junk drawer' has three problems. It skips his years on the Millers' counter, which misstates the backstory. It relies on the bakery bin, which bakers aren't told about in onboarding or earlier in this lesson. And 'bin to drawer' doesn't clearly read as 'headed the WRONG way,' so a stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: A callback only works if its setup came earlier in this lesson or conversation. Bakers know he spent years in a junk drawer, from onboarding.

findings.problem: 'Jerusalem is a famous queen now' only recaps verses 13 and 14. The card tells nothing from verse 15, yet it cites Ezekiel 16:15.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: The question says God 'gives Jerusalem over to the daughters of the Philistines.' The text says God 'gave you over to the desire of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines' (Ezekiel 16:27). Dropping 'the desire of' changes what the text says.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: 'Then God hands her over to those very same lovers' tells as happening now what God says He will do: 'I will deliver you into the hands of your lovers' (Ezekiel 16:39).

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: 'What do Jerusalem's lovers do to the mounds...' asks about a present action. The text gives a future judgment: 'they will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines' (Ezekiel 16:39).

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: 'They strip off her clothes, take her fine jewelry and leave her naked and bare' tells as happening now what the text says 'They will' do (Ezekiel 16:39).

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The statement says the lovers 'leave her alone' once they've taken everything, which treats the judgment as already happening. The text is a future prophecy: 'They will bring a mob against you' (Ezekiel 16:40).

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: 'A mob comes with stones and swords. They burn down her houses...' tells as happening now what the text says 'They will bring' and 'they will burn down' (Ezekiel 16:40-41).

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The 'story isn't over' line, 'And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend,' copies the doc's example line almost word for word instead of being a new line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
